abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces the Interactive Computation Model (ICM), a novel theoretical framework that fundamentally reconceptualizes computation as an ongoing dialogue between computational agents rather than a static input-output transformation. Unlike the classical Turing machine model, ICM captures the essential characteristics of modern computing environments where programs continuously interact with external data sources, users, and other programs. We establish a comprehensive complexity theory within ICM, defining interactive complexity classes that properly contain their classical counterparts while maintaining meaningful captures of efficient computation. Our central contribution is the Interactive Polynomial Hierarchy (IPH), which we prove exhibits a distinctive alternating structure fundamentally different from the polynomial hierarchy. We demonstrate that several natural problems that are believed to be hard in the classical setting admit surprisingly efficient interactive algorithms, challenging prevailing complexity assumptions. Furthermore, we establish novel connections between interactive computation and game theory, showing that the fixed-point semantics of ICM naturally encode strategic interactions. This work opens a new frontier in theoretical computer science, providing both conceptual tools for reasoning about modern computational paradigms and concrete complexity-theoretic results that advance our fundamental understanding of computation's limits and possibilities.

We present a significant advance in understanding the complexity of combinatorial optimization by proving that the Maximum Cut problem admits a (0.8784+ε)-approximation algorithm running in subexponential time, substantially improving upon the classical Goemans-Williamson result. Our approach introduces a semidefinite programming hierarchy with rounded constraints that captures the structure of graphs excluded from a minor, enabling an improved approximation ratio for these graph classes. We prove that for any fixed excluded minor H, Max-Cut on H-free graphs can be approximated to within a factor arbitrarily close to 1 in subexponential time, resolving an open problem that has resisted progress for over two decades. The key technical innovation is a new rounding scheme that exploits spectral properties of matrices in the hierarchy, combined with a refined analysis of the correlation clustering structure. Additionally, we establish tight lower bounds under the Unique Games Conjecture, showing that our approximation factors are optimal for this graph class. Our results have immediate implications for related optimization problems, including Minimum Bisection and Edge Multiway Cut, for which we derive improved approximation algorithms using the same underlying techniques. The analysis relies on novel connections between semidefinite optimization hierarchies and graph minor theory, providing a framework that may be applicable to other combinatorial optimization problems.

This paper presents Chronos, a distributed consensus system that fundamentally abandons the traditional leader-based paradigm in favor of a novel naturally leaderless coordination mechanism. Unlike existing Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols that rely on leader election or rotating coordinator schemes, Chronos achieves consensus through an elegantly simple localルール-based approach where correct processes reach agreement by executing identical state transition rules based solely on locally observed message histories. We formalize the correctness conditions of this coordination model and prove that Chronos guarantees safety and liveness in partially synchronous networks with up to f < n/3 Byzantine processes, matching the optimal resilience bound. The architectural innovation lies in replacing global coordination with local rule evaluation, enabling unprecedented scalability characteristics: throughput scales linearly with the number of participating nodes, and latency remains essentially constant regardless of network size. We present a complete specification of the Chronos protocol, prove its correctness through a novel invariant-based argument, and provide an implementation that achieves over 100,000 transactions per second in a 100-node deployment with sub-millisecond consensus latency. The system requires no coordination infrastructure beyond basic point-to-point messaging, making it particularly suitable for federated and multi-stakeholder deployments where centralized components are undesirable. This work challenges the prevailing assumption that distributed consensus inherently requires leader-based coordination.

We present CrypTen, a comprehensive framework for privacy-preserving machine learning that achieves orders-of-magnitude performance improvements over existing secure computation systems while maintaining rigorous cryptographic security guarantees. CrypTen introduces a novel abstraction layer that maps high-level tensor operations to optimized secure computation protocols, eliminating the traditional compilation overhead that has limited practical adoption of cryptographic ML techniques. Our system supports a comprehensive set of neural network operations including convolution, batch normalization, and recurrent layers, enabling secure evaluation of complex architectures including ResNet, LSTM, and Transformer models. The key technical contribution is a protocol design that leverages GPU-accelerated secret sharing over the Ring-LWE lattice, achieving 50-100x speedup for linear algebra operations compared to prior art. We present detailed benchmarks demonstrating that CrypTen can evaluate a secure ResNet-50 image classifier in 230 milliseconds on commodity hardware, compared to 47 seconds required by the best prior system. For natural language processing applications, we show that secure BERT inference completes in under 2 seconds. Beyond performance, we provide a formal security proof establishing that CrypTen achieves security against malicious adversaries under the standard universal composability framework. The system includes comprehensive tooling for secure model training, enabling privacy-preserving collaborative learning scenarios previously considered impractical.
